Traditional relational classification methods, such as collective classification in Markov logic networks or probabilistic relational models, often couple feature learning and label inference in one joint model. They then rely on iterative approximate inference (loopy belief propagation, Gibbs sampling, mean-field updates) that must be rerun until convergence, and labels and relational structure are estimated together. The proposed approach, as the question describes it, separates these stages. It first learns representations of entities and relations without labels, in an unsupervised way, and then performs classification on those representations, typically in a single feed-forward pass rather than an iterative message-passing loop. This separation provides practical advantages: inference is faster and more scalable to large graphs, it avoids convergence and approximation problems of loopy inference, the learned representations can be reused across tasks, and the classifier can be trained or swapped independently of the unsupervised component.
